value_text: After the strike on the Taman 500 kV substation, power failed around 01:45 in Simferopol, Sevastopol, Kerch, Feodosia and Yalta; Russian-installed Sevastopol authorities said restrictions were lifted after about 90 minutes, though the grid stayed unstable and some settlements remained without power. No consumer count is given.

Reuters: Orsknefteorgsintez ceased processing on 11 Aug after a fire from the drone attack. Nameplate ~5.76 Mt/yr (~115,200 bbl/d); in 2024 it processed 4.2 Mt of crude. (Moscow Times separately cites 6.6 Mt/yr; conflict preserved.)

Moscow Times: with the refinery fully shut, the Orenburg governor said the region would rely on fuel trucked in, and that 80% of the region's 287 filling stations were operational, priority to emergency vehicles.

Moscow Times: the Orenburg governor said repairs could take up to six months because shrapnel damaged key infrastructure hard to replace under Western sanctions. A projection, not an observed restart.

Meduza (industry data): the 14 July overnight strike disabled both primary crude distillation units at Salavat -- CDU-6 (17,140 t/day) and CDU-4 (11,430 t/day) -- taking the complex offline. The plant was ~2.7% of Russia's total refining throughput in 2024.

World Oil: after the 24 June strike forced the Orenburg GPP to suspend intake of Karachaganak raw gas, output at Kazakhstan's Karachaganak field was cut by more than a quarter -- 34,000 t/day normally to 25,000 t/day (~180,000 bbl/d). Field oil and gas output are linked. (Interfax gives different figures; both preserved.)

Interfax (citing KazMunayGas): Karachaganak output was cut by 9,000 t/day on 26 June -- to ~28,000 from ~31,000 -- after the Orenburg plant incident, and as of 30 June was not yet fully restored. (Baseline differs from World Oil; both reported unmerged.)

Reuters (via Ukrinform): the early-Feb 2025 strike halted fuel output at Gazprom's Astrakhan GPP; the damaged gas-condensate unit has ~3 Mt/yr capacity, and industry sources said it might only resume in weeks or months. (Value is the affected unit's annual capacity; the halt is the observed effect.)

Reuters (via RBC-Ukraine): the CDU-4 (AVT-4) primary unit at LUKOIL's Perm refinery was out from 30 April after the 29 April strike/fire; a 7 May strike shut three more primary units and completely halted processing. The refinery ran ~12.6 Mt of crude in 2024 (~250,000 bbl/d).

Hydrocarbon Processing (citing Reuters/industry): Rosneft's Syzran refinery halted processing after the 18 April attack, shutting primary unit CDU-6, which is >70% of plant capacity. Capacity 8.5 Mt/yr (~170,000 bbl/d).

Militarnyi: LUKOIL's Volgograd refinery suspended operations after the strike (this source dates it to the night of 29 May 2026 -- 2-3 days before the incident's 2026-06-01 label; likely the same event). Primary distillation unit No. 1 (~40% of capacity) stopped, as did units 5 and 6. Capacity 14.8 Mt/yr of products (~300,000 bbl/d).

Reuters (via Moscow Times): as of 20 May 2026, refineries fully halted or significantly reduced after drone strikes totalled >83 Mt/yr of capacity (~238,000 t/day) -- nearly a quarter of Russia's total refining -- accounting for >30% of gasoline output and ~25% of diesel output.
Kyiv Independent (citing the Financial Times): Ukrainian strikes had hit at least 16 of Russia's 38 oil refineries since Aug 2025, pushing Russian diesel exports to their lowest level since 2020.

Moscow Times: Russia extended its gasoline export ban (exporters and producers) through 31 Dec 2025, and barred resellers from selling diesel, marine fuel and other gas oils abroad through end-2025 (direct producers exempt) -- a policy response to strike-driven domestic fuel tightness.

Moscow Times: a Kommersant estimate put the gasoline shortage at 20% (~400,000 t/month). The same article reports as observed fact that two Far East regions and annexed Crimea introduced ration cards for buying gasoline.
